https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: The best practice for investigating potential bodies inside things like wheelie bins and suitcases is not to open it, but to x-ray it, an expert says. Photograph: Kevin Frayer/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The best practice for investigating potential bodies inside things like wheelie bins and suitcases is not to open it, but to x-ray it, an expert says. Photograph: Kevin Frayer/Getty Images Australian police and policing A ‘body’ found in a suitcase was actually a sex doll. How did NSW police get it so wrong? Officers – correctly – may not have fully unzipped the bag containing the lifelike doll to avoid destroying evidence, one expert says Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Kat Wong Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.03 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Revelations that a “body” found inside a suitcase was actually a sex doll may have been embarrassing for police, but experts say officers followed the correct procedure. New South Wales police on Sunday were called to Oallen, a town near Goulburn, after two members of the public found a suitcase containing what they believed to be human remains, dumped on the side of the road. A police statement released on Sunday said the body was believed to be female, and the bag was sent to the forensic medicine laboratory. ‘Body’ found in suitcase near Goulburn was actually lifelike doll with ‘bruises and grazes’ Read more But after forensic examinations on Monday morning, it was confirmed the “body” was actually a life-like doll dressed in clothes that had hair, a nose piercing, markings that resembled bruises and grazes. While former NSW police officer Vincent Hurley said the discovery was “amusing in hindsight”, investigators had done the right thing. “Police have been blamed over the years, and rightly so, for tunnel vision,” Hurley, a criminologist, told Guardian Australia. “Can you imagine if it was a real body and they just go unzip the bag and say, ‘we’ll have a poke’? “They did the right thing, it’s embarrassing, yes, but they followed procedure.” When police arrive at a reported crime scene, they generally try not to contaminate it, Hurley said. This means they may not have unzipped the bag the entire way to confirm a potential body, because doing so could destroy any fibres or blood that may have been on the zipper. The best practice for investigating potential bodies inside things like wheelie bins and suitcases is not to open it, but to X-ray it, Paola Magni, a Murdoch University forensic science associate professor, said. Even after realising they had a doll, forensic examiners likely would have had to fully continue inspecting it for traces of evidence like semen or other DNA in case it was associated with another suspicious case. “It’s a doll, but if it’s connected to another crime, they can use that opportunity to link it to something suspect,” says Magni, an expert in decomposition. “Any potentially suspicious situation has to be treated with the best practice in forensic investigation. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion “They did the right thing, they investigated it step-by-step.” Hurley also said objects like sex dolls could be “incredibly lifelike” and noted the bodies of real murder victims were often found in confined places like car boots, suitcases and barrels. “It’s not unusual to be in a suitcase, it’s just unusual that it turned out to be a plastic doll,” he said. Crimes around sex dolls are generally rare, but in Australia possessing a child-like sex doll is an offence and police have previously charged people after intercepting air cargo found to contain such items. However, the one discovered on Sunday is not believed to be childlike and police investigations into it have concluded. At her press conference on Monday, Superintendent Linda Bradbury maintained police had “no regrets”. “Our police have undertaken the processes that we do to maintain integrity in such serious crime, to a T, and I do commend people for that,” she said. Bradbury also confirmed the members of the public who discovered the suitcase had made the right decision by pulling over, peeking inside, and calling as soon as they believed it was something suspicious. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/08/hout.text: Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday they targeted King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh with a ballistic missile, as the group escalates its strikes on airports across the neighbouring kingdom.There was no immediate confirmation of the strike or any damage or casualties from Saudi Arabia at this time.Several explosions echoed across Riyadh on Thursday, according to witnesses.Diplomats were instructed to shelter in place in their respective embassies, as witnesses said international schools were also taking precautions.An earlier drone attack on the same airport killed one person, with another two killed in a separate strike on the airport in the southwestern city of Abha, Riyadh said on Thursday, as flight delays continued into the second day.The attack on Abha airport killed Moroccan and Algerian residents and wounded 28 other people, while the attack on King Khalid airport killed a Sudanese national and wounded eight other people, officials said.The Saudi General Authority for Civil Aviation did not blame any party for the attacks at the two international airports.In a subsequent statement, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the strikes and vowed a response."The brutal attacks by the terrorist Houthi militia on civilian and civilian objects in the kingdom, most recently targeting (the two airports) will not go unpunished," it wrote on X.The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, Major General Turki al-Malki, said forces intercepted a ballistic missile north of Riyadh and destroyed a platform in Yemen’s capital of Sana'a that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital.The group formally known as Ansar Allah has claimed repeated attacks targeting Saudi airports in recent days, along with salvos aimed at critical infrastructure and military sites across the kingdom.Strikes on Saudi facilities pose a threat to crucial shipping alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic has been curtailed due to the Iran war.Saudi Arabia has also accused the Houthis of targeting Islam's holiest sites in Mecca and Medina, allegations the group rejected as "fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal al-Saud regime."The Houthis are Zaydi Shia Muslims, a specific branch of Islam historically rooted in northern Yemen that is theologically distinct from both the Twelver Shia Islam dominant in Iran and Saudi Arabia's Wahhabi-influenced Sunni tradition.Any confirmed attack on either Mecca or Medina would put the perpetrators beyond the pale in the eyes of virtually the entire Muslim world, Shia and Sunni alike.Houthi strikes have further escalated as Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces launched a major ground and air offensive aimed at retaking territory that the group seized a month ago along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and on the Bab el-Mandeb strait.On Monday, officials said forces of the Saudi-led coalition recaptured several key areas around the strait, through which about 12% of global trade transits.“The Houthis believe that they can maximise Saudi economic costs and compel Saudi Arabia to surrender to Houthi demands by striking civilian infrastructure, such as oil facilities and airports,” the Washington-based Institute for the Study of War think tank wrote in an analysis.The fighting in Yemen has in recent weeks become the most active front of the wider regional war, which for months has seen violence repeatedly shift focus across the beleaguered Middle East.More than 200,000 people have been displaced since the Yemen war escalated again in July, according to UN data.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy4.text: Image source, Vantor/BBC By Soram Cheon ,Â BBC Korean Â and Â Aghnia Adzkia ,Â East Asia Visual Journalism Published 4 hours ago An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year. What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end. After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula. This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family. It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC. The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size. "In winter, they would keep them at the shipyard. When summer came, they would bring them out and move them to Kim Jong Un's villa or towards Kalma, and use them for swimming and recreation," says Ri Jong Ho. Ri was once an official at the Workers' Party's Office 39, which is believed to be involved in raising and managing foreign currency for the leadership. The wealth of those who sit at the top of the secretive North Korean dictatorship is just as hard to pin down as the country's economic figures. The United Nations and others rely on estimates to classify North Korea as one of the world's poorest countries, with an especially large military budget that funds a sanctioned nuclear programme. Most North Koreans, according to a 2025 UN report, live under "systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations" with total state control, widespread forced labour, and chronic food shortages that leave an estimated 40% of the population undernourished. But the regime has long been known to live in luxury. We don't know the cost of the vessels seen in the satellite imagery, but comparable luxury yachts run from tens of millions to over $100m (Â£75m). Kim's much smaller, 29-metre Princess yacht was previously estimated to be worth about $7m. While vessel locations alone cannot definitively establish the family's whereabouts, their movements - which overlap with gaps in Kim's public appearances - point to activities that would otherwise remain out of public view. Wonsan is where Kim Jong Un spent part of his childhood with his mother, according to biographers and intelligence reports, and one expert told the BBC the city has been associated with the family since his father Kim Jong Il's rule. A defector who served for 13 years guarding residences used by then leader Kim Jong Il - through the 1990s to the early 2000s - told the BBC the villas around Wonsan were used as a retreat by the elite. He recalls seeing dozens of children and teens waterskiing during summer. North Korean state media rarely publishes reports about Kim being on holiday, instead framing such visits as official inspections or guidance. But defectors interviewed by the BBC appeared to be aware that the family spent holidays in Wonsan, suggesting that at least some North Koreans knew about it. North Korean state media also claims Wonsan is home to high-rise hotels, restaurants, shops, sports facilities and water parks, and can accommodate nearly 20,000 visitors. State media and Russian outlets have published images of small groups of Russian tourists visiting the Wonsan Kalma resort, which opened in July 2025. Although developed to attract foreign visitors, the resort is also open to local tourists. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, North Korean tourists on a beach in Kalma A South Korean news report, citing an unnamed source, says some locals were offered four-night tour packages for around $100, a substantial sum for most North Koreans. The country's per capita GDP - around $667 in 2024, according to the UN - is a small fraction of South Korea's $36,227. For the majority of North Koreans, holidays are out of reach. And while a growing middle class does exist, they might not have much time for leisure. Defectors told the BBC that workers, office employees and cooperative farmers are legally entitled to 14 days of annual leave, but this is rarely followed. Taking consecutive days off to travel is unusual. People typically take weekend trips or travel during national holidays instead of designated "summer holidays". Even if leave is granted, travel itself is restricted, with official permission required for people to travel outside their city or county. Moving freely is sometimes as much a luxury as the holiday itself. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Ordinary North Koreans struggle to earn a decent living The BBC tracked four large vessels around Wonsan, measuring approximately 50m, 55m, 60m and 80m. All four vessels repeatedly appeared around Kim's Wonsan villa this year. The largest vessel showed the clearest activity, moving from the dock to the waters off the Kalma Peninsula, where it has been since July. Two of the other vessels - 50m and 55m - were repeatedly seen until the end of August around Tae and Sin islands, close to Wonsan. Satellite images also showed four smaller boats alongside the 50m vessel. Image source, Vantor Image caption, The 50m vessel was seen in waters near Tae island on 4 July 2026. Satellite imagery expert Jeong Seong-hak said the smaller boats ferried people, fuel and supplies to the larger vessel, adding that small islands like Tae and Sin offered "secluded maritime retreats where privacy can be maintained away from public view". The 60m vessel was repeatedly seen near Kim's Wonsan villa until as recently as last week. Though North Korea has never publicly disclosed the vessels' official ownership, BBC's analysis of historical satellite imagery found a large vessel with the same distinctive characteristics in Wonsan in 2002, when Kim Jong Il ruled North Korea. Former NBA star Dennis Rodman, who visited the North in 2013, told The Sun that he had spent much of his seven-day visit with Kim Jong Un around Wonsan, where they went jet-skiing and horse riding. He also described a 60m vessel they used as a cross between a ferry and a Disney boat. It is not clear if this is the same 60m boat pictured in the above satellite imagery. To most North Koreans, the life lived by the Kims and others who support the regime would seem not just extravagant but unimaginable. Especially because state propaganda is dedicated to presenting the "supreme leader" as a selfless man who always puts the nation first. "Kim Jong Un is supposed to be a 'leader of the people'," Ri Jong Ho says, "yet he has four luxury vessels like these while ordinary people are struggling just to get one meal a day." https://www.kyivpost.com/post/86669.text: War Ukraine World North America Latin America Europe Eastern Europe Middle East Africa Asia Economy Business Technology Finance Energy Agriculture Videos Podcasts Analysis Corruption Watch Opinions Culture Reviews History Sports Classifieds Spotlight Cartoons EN UK Finland War in Ukraine Europe Finland Approves 35th Military Aid Package for Ukraine In brief: Finnish President Alexander Stubb approved the delivery of Finland’s 35th military aid package to Ukraine on Friday, Oct. 9, following an urgent appeal from Kyiv. Valued at approximately €1 million ($1.1 million), the shipment draws a single defense product from military stockpiles, bringing total Finnish defense assistance to €3.6 billion ($4 billion) as preparations begin for a broader upcoming package. by Kyiv Post | Oct. 10, 2026, 11:39 am Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Finnish President Alexander Stubb at a press conference during a meeting at the Norwegian Prime Minister’s Office in Oslo, Oct 8, 2026. (Photo by Ole Berg-Rusten / NTB / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Finnish President Alexander Stubb approved the delivery of Finland’s 35th defense materiel assistance package to Ukraine on Friday, Oct. 9, acting on a formal proposal submitted by the government. The newly allocated assistance package carries an estimated valuation of approximately €1 million ($1.1million) and consists of a single defense product drawn directly from the operational stockpiles of the Finnish Defence Forces. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . With the latest tranche, the cumulative value of defense materiel delivered by Helsinki to Kyiv since the start of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion reached €3.6 billion ($4 billion). Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen stated that the decision was expedited following an urgent appeal transmitted by Ukrainian defense authorities. Advertisement “Finland speeded up this decision to deliver on an urgent request from Ukraine. We will not close our eyes to Ukrainians’ hour of need. Instead, we will stand with Ukraine and continue our materiel assistance deliveries,” Häkkänen said in an official statement released by the Ministry of Defence. Finnish defense authorities confirmed that preparatory work has already commenced for an upcoming, more extensive military assistance package. Citing operational security considerations and the imperative to protect delivery corridors, the ministry declined to disclose specific technical details regarding the weapon type, transportation methods, or transfer timetables, noting that the allocation balanced Ukraine’s operational requirements against the territorial readiness of the Finnish military. Other Topics of Interest Russia Exploits School Knife Attacks for Disinformation Polish Defense Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz warned hostile actors weaponized a wave of school stabbings in Mazovia that left one dead and 11 wounded. Strategic deterrence The emergency defense allocation aligns with public statements delivered by President Stubb at the annual Helsinki Security Forum , where the Finnish leader emphasized that Western capitals must answer Russian pressure by expanding military backing for Ukraine. Addressing an international assembly alongside Moldovan President Maia Sandu and President Volodymyr Zelensky , Stubb argued that Moscow’s escalatory hybrid campaigns across Europe – encompassing physical sabotage, recurring cyber disruptions, and cognitive warfare – demand unified collective resistance rather than diplomatic hesitation. Advertisement “The more you intimidate, the more you threaten, the more we’re going to end up supporting Ukraine,” Stubb told the forum, warning that European governments must recognize Russian hybrid actions not as isolated disruptions, but as an institutionalized campaign designed to weaken political support for Kyiv. Stubb highlighted that Russia’s strategic calculations have consistently backfired, noting that Moscow’s attempt to halt NATO’s footprint prompted Finland and Sweden to abandon decades of military non-alignment and accede to the transatlantic alliance. Finland, which maintains a 1,340-kilometer (830-mile) frontier with Russia, formally joined NATO in April 2023, while Sweden acceded in March 2024. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-trust.text: LISBON — The European Union should work “only with very trusted partners” on artificial intelligence microchips, its tech chief said Tuesday, just days after revelations of a spy scandal rocked industry leader Nvidia. “When we speak about very critical technologies, like AI semiconductors and quantum technologies, cybersecurity, satellites ... it’s very important that we are working very closely only with very trusted partners,” said Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission’s executive vice president for tech sovereignty. She made the comments in an interview with POLITICO at the Web Summit tech fair in Lisbon, when asked about Europe’s reliance on Nvidia. It is Virkkunen’s first public comment since Nvidia opened an internal investigation into whether its CEO was targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation. Top executive Jensen Huang admitted to an affair following a reported relationship with an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed whom the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy. Advertisement Advertisement Virkkunen did not detail whether she considered Nvidia less trustworthy since news of the spy scandal broke. When asked who she considers trusted partners, she described the U.S. as the EU’s traditionally “closest partner when it comes to security and technology,” suggesting the bloc has no intention of blaming the U.S. but would prefer to collaborate to plug the security gap. In “limited areas of technologies,” it is important to ensure that “we don’t have that kind of technological leakages,” the EU tech chief said. “We want to really keep the business secrets in Europe.” Europe is heavily reliant on Nvidia chips, since it has little production or design capacity for AI chips of its own — something that the EU aims to correct for through an industrial policy push into chipmaking called the European Chips Act. “It’s true that currently Europe is very dependent on AI chips on a few American companies and that's why it's important also that we are building up our own capacity to also design and also manufacture more advanced [chips] and also AI chips in the coming years," Virkkunen said. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
